title: Knowledge and Perception in Plato
orientation: This chapter examines Plato's Theaetetus, in which Socrates and the young Theaetetus test and ultimately reject the definition 'knowledge is perception.' Russell uses the dialogue as an occasion to work out, in his own terms, what perception actually is and why mathematical and logical knowledge cannot be derived from the senses -- a question that matters because it sets the terms for the empiricism-versus-rationalism debate that runs through the rest of Western philosophy.
historical_background: The Theaetetus is a mature Platonic dialogue, written after Plato had already developed the theory of Ideas, though that theory is deliberately kept in the background here. Russell notes that the view that real knowledge concerns only concepts, not the senses, is 'perhaps traceable to Parmenides,' whose rejection of change and multiplicity lies behind Plato's discomfort with a world of flux. The dialogue also targets two specific rival doctrines current in Plato's Athens: the relativism of the sophist Protagoras ('man is the measure of all things') and the extreme flux-doctrine attributed to disciples of Heraclitus at Ephesus.
philosophical_problems: If each person's perceptions are equally valid (Protagoras), does truth become purely relative to the perceiver?
If everything is in constant flux (Heraclitus), can words and judgements have any fixed meaning at all?
Can the mind know things such as existence, likeness, and number that no single sense-organ perceives?
Is mathematical knowledge derived from sense-perception, or is it independent of it?

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Author of the Theaetetus; Russell examines his critique of the definition 'knowledge is perception,' his handling of Protagorean relativism and Heraclitean flux, and his final argument that knowledge requires apprehending existence, likeness, and number, none of which is perceived through any sense-organ.

philosophers_discussed.name: Theaetetus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The young mathematician who proposes, in the dialogue named for him, the first and only definition of knowledge Russell considers: 'knowledge is nothing but perception.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Protagoras
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: His doctrine 'man is the measure of all things' is identified by Socrates with the view that knowledge is perception; the dialogue tests and largely refutes it, though Socrates (on Protagoras's behalf) offers a proto-pragmatist defense that judgements can be 'better' though not 'truer.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Heraclitus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: His doctrine that everything is always changing is imported into the argument to explain perception as an unstable interaction between a changing object and a changing sense-organ; pushed to an extreme by his 'disciples at Ephesus,' the doctrine is shown to make coherent speech about perception impossible.

philosophers_discussed.name: Parmenides
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Mentioned only briefly: Socrates refuses to discuss him, calling him 'a reverend and awful figure' and 'one being whom I respect above all,' which Russell reads as revealing Plato's own preference for a static universe over the Heraclitean flux he has been provisionally defending.

core_concepts.name: Knowledge as perception (Theaetetus's definition)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The idea that to know something just is to perceive it -- so that whatever seems true to me, through my senses, simply is true for me.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Theaetetus's proposed definition: 'one who knows something is perceiving the thing that he knows, and... knowledge is nothing but perception,' which Socrates identifies with Protagoras's doctrine that 'man is the measure of all things.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the first of several definitions of knowledge tested and rejected in the dialogue, and it forces Plato to work out, by contrast, what more than perception knowledge must involve.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Proposed by Theaetetus at the start of Plato's dialogue of that name.
examples: Socrates finding wine sweet when well but sour when ill, illustrating perception as relative to the state of the percipient
objections: It collapses into Protagorean relativism, making one man's judgement as good as another's
It cannot account for knowledge of existence, likeness, or number, none of which is given through any single sense
Memory must be added to perception even to make the definition plausible
competing_positions: Plato's own (largely implicit) view that real knowledge concerns unchanging concepts, not the shifting deliverances of sense
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets the template for the empiricist-versus-rationalist dispute over whether all knowledge derives from sense-experience.

core_concepts.name: Protagorean relativism ('man is the measure of all things')
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The claim that a thing simply is, for each person, however it appears to that person -- so there is no independent fact of the matter beyond individual appearance.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that any given thing 'is to me such as it appears to me, and is to you such as it appears to you,' making individual perception (and, on the extended interpretation, individual judgement) the final standard of truth.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It threatens to make all inference, and not merely perception, purely personal, which Plato treats as leading to an intolerable intellectual anarchy.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Attributed to the sophist Protagoras and examined in Plato's Theaetetus.
examples: The objection that pigs and baboons, being percipients, would equally be 'measures of all things' on Protagoras's principle
The suggestion, on Protagoras's behalf, that one judgement cannot be truer than another but can be 'better,' in having better consequences -- which Russell notes anticipates pragmatism
objections: If each man is equally wise, Protagoras is no wiser than a fool, and those who think Protagoras wrong have as much right to be believed as he does
A doctor's forecast of the course of an illness shows he genuinely knows more about a patient's future than the patient does, so not all judgements are equally good measures
competing_positions: Plato's insistence that inference (as opposed to bare percepts) requires an impersonal standard of correctness
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes it foreshadows pragmatism, particularly the idea (which he attributes to F. C. S. Schiller's admiration of Protagoras) that a belief's value lies in its consequences rather than in a fixed truth.

core_concepts.name: Universal flux (Heraclitean doctrine applied to sense-objects)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The idea that everything perceptible is constantly changing in every respect, so that a thing is never quite the same from one instant to the next.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, pushed to an extreme by 'the bright youths of Ephesus,' that everything is always changing both by locomotion and by change of every quality at once, so that no percept can be called 'seeing' rather than 'not-seeing,' nor any statement true rather than false.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Combined with 'knowledge is perception,' it implies that knowledge is only of what becomes, never of what is -- and, pressed to its extreme, undermines the very possibility of stating anything, including the doctrine of flux itself.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced to Heraclitus and radicalized by his Ephesian disciples, as reported in the Theaetetus.
examples: The claim that 'this is white' cannot be truly said, since the thing will have ceased to be white before the sentence is finished
Russell's aside that modern quantum physics allows change of qualities without change of substance -- something not fatal to science, contrary to what Plato assumed
objections: If everything, including the meanings of words, is in perpetual flux, no assertion can be definite or true rather than false
Aristotle later objected that unrestricted flux would make even locomotion impossible, since a moving thing must remain the same thing while it moves
competing_positions: Parmenides' denial of all change, alluded to but not developed in this dialogue
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: The puzzle of relational statements it raises (e.g. Socrates being both 'tall' and 'short' relative to different people) Russell says 'puzzled... most of the great philosophers down to Hegel.'

core_concepts.name: Percept versus judgement of perception
core_concepts.plain_explanation: A raw sensation (a patch of colour, a sound) is not yet a belief and cannot be true or false; only once it is 'filled out' with words, memories, and comparisons does it become a judgement capable of truth or falsehood.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's own distinction: a 'percept' is a mere occurrence, belonging equally to physics and psychology, neither true nor false; a 'judgement of perception' is the percept filled out with words and memory, and is the proper referent when we say 'knowledge is perception' -- more accurately, 'knowledge is judgements of perception.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It allows Russell to rescue part of what is right in the perception theory of knowledge while showing exactly why bare percepts cannot themselves constitute knowledge.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Introduced by Russell in this chapter as his own analytical tool for assessing Plato's argument.
examples: Seeing two shades of colour and judging 'A is like B,' where the likeness is part of what is given, not something added purely by the mind
competing_positions: Plato's assumption that we perceive through, rather than merely with, our sense-organs, and that comparison and existence require a wholly separate mental faculty

core_concepts.name: 'Existence' as bad syntax (the critique of predicating existence of things)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: It is nonsense to say of a particular thing, pointed to directly, that 'this exists'; we can only sensibly say that a description ('the largest lion in the Zoo') applies to something, i.e. that there is an x satisfying it.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's argument that 'exists' is a predicate applicable only to descriptions (incomplete or complete), not to names or to bare percepts; 'lions exist' means 'there are lions,' i.e. "'x is a lion' is true for a suitable x," and one cannot coherently add, of a perceived particular, 'and that exists.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It dismantles Plato's claim that the mind directly apprehends 'existence' as a special object alongside sound and colour, and it also undercuts the ontological argument for the existence of God, which trades on the same confusion.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Russell's own logical analysis, developed in this chapter as a response to Plato's argument in the Theaetetus.
examples: Taking a child to the zoo and saying 'look, that's a lion' proves lions exist without needing to add 'and you can see that that exists'
competing_positions: Plato's view that 'existence,' like likeness and number, is among the things the mind apprehends by itself, without any sense-organ
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly relevant, Russell notes, 'to other matters such as the ontological argument for the existence of the Deity.'

core_concepts.name: Numbers as logical fictions
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Words like 'two' or 'ten' do not name any real thing that percepts contain; when a statement using them is properly spelled out, the number-word disappears, replaced by patterns of 'there is an a... there is a b... a is not b.'
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's claim that number-words are 'formal': what verifies 'there are two so-and-sos' is a common logical form shared by many different facts, not a common constituent (unlike, e.g., a proper name that always refers to the same particular thing); properly analysed, a sentence like 'I have two hands' contains no constituent corresponding to the word 'two.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It lets Russell agree with Plato that pure mathematics is not derived from perception (since it consists of tautologies about symbols) while denying that number designates a Platonic Idea perceived by a special faculty of mind.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Russell in this chapter, drawing on his broader logical analysis of number (referred to elsewhere in his work).
examples: 'I have two hands' analysed as: there is an a and a b, a is not identical with b, and 'x is a hand of mine' is true only when x is a or x is b
The fallacy of arguing 'the earth has one satellite, namely the moon, therefore the moon is one,' compared to 'the Apostles were twelve; Peter was an apostle; therefore Peter was twelve'
competing_positions: Plato's suggestion that 'ten' or 'one,' like 'existence,' names something the mind grasps directly and which is common to sound and colour alike

arguments.title: Extreme flux undermines the coherence of speech about perception
premises: If knowledge is perception, and everything is in Heraclitean flux, then whatever is perceived is always becoming something else, never simply 'is.'

If a thing changes in every respect at every instant, then 'seeing' is perpetually changing into 'not-seeing,' and any assertion made about it will have become false before the sentence describing it is finished.
arguments.conclusion: Under the extreme doctrine of flux, no assertion -- including 'perception is knowledge' -- can be definitely true rather than false, so the identification of knowledge with perception collapses into unintelligibility.
arguments.explanation: Plato's dialogue pushes the Heraclitean premise to its logical extreme to show that the perception theory of knowledge, once combined with universal flux, destroys the very possibility of stable assertion that any theory of knowledge requires.
objections: Russell notes this shows only that word-meanings must be fixed 'at least for a time,' which is compatible with a great deal of flux -- it does not refute a moderate doctrine of change
implications: Some minimal constancy of meaning is a precondition for discourse and knowledge, whatever else may be in flux

arguments.title: Knowledge requires apprehending existence, likeness, and number, which no sense-organ perceives
premises: We perceive sound through hearing and colour through sight, but no single sense-organ perceives that sound and colour both exist, or that they are unlike each other, or how many of them there are.
Yet knowing that two things exist, or are alike or unlike, or number two, is essential to knowledge.
Only the mind, using 'its own instrumentality' rather than any bodily organ, can reach existence, likeness, unlikeness, and number.
Without reaching existence, one cannot reach truth.
arguments.conclusion: Perception alone -- since it 'has no part in apprehending truth, since it has none in apprehending existence' -- cannot be knowledge; knowledge consists in reflection, not in bare sense-impressions.
arguments.explanation: This is Plato's final and, in Russell's view, most serious argument in the dialogue against identifying knowledge with perception: some of what knowledge requires (existence, comparison, number) is simply not delivered by any sense-organ, so knowledge must be more than perception.
objections: Russell argues likeness and unlikeness can be part of the perceptual datum itself (a 'judgement of perception'), so Plato's argument here ignores the cortex and wrongly assumes all sense-organs are at the body's surface
Russell argues Plato's treatment of 'existence' is simply bad syntax: 'exists' applies only to descriptions, not to things pointed out directly, so there is no special faculty needed to apprehend it

Russell agrees mathematics is independent of perception, but denies this supports Plato's general conclusion, since propositions of enumeration (e.g. 'I have ten fingers') are, in the relevant sense, dependent on perception once properly analysed
implications: Only formal knowledge (logic and pure mathematics) is genuinely independent of perception; Plato's arguments extending this to all other knowledge are, in Russell's judgement, fallacious -- though this does not prove his conclusion false, only unproven

arguments.title: The doctor's foreknowledge refutes strict Protagorean equality of judgement
premises: If each man's judgement is as good as another's, then no one can know more about the future than anyone else.
A doctor genuinely foretells the future course of a patient's illness better than the patient can.
Statesmen sometimes turn out to have judged the future needs of the state better than others who disagreed with them.
arguments.conclusion: A wise man is a better measure of things than a fool, so the doctrine that each man is the measure of all things cannot be sustained without qualification.
arguments.explanation: This argument targets specifically the extension of Protagorean relativism from bare perception (where each man's percepts are, in a sense, equally 'his own') to inference and judgement about the future, where some people are demonstrably more reliable than others.
implications: There must be some impersonal standard of correctness for inference, even if percepts themselves are irreducibly private

key_distinctions: Percept (a bare occurrence, neither true nor false) vs. judgement of perception (percept plus words/memory, capable of truth or falsehood)
Knowledge of what becomes (sense-objects, on the Heraclitean view) vs. knowledge of what is
Pure mathematics (tautological, formal, independent of perception) vs. propositions of enumeration (partly dependent on perception)
Percepts, which are inescapably private to each perceiver, vs. inferences, which Plato insists must answer to an impersonal standard
'Exists' as applied to a description (legitimate) vs. 'exists' as applied directly to a perceived particular (nonsense, on Russell's analysis)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell traces the view that only concepts, not sense-data, can be objects of real knowledge back to Parmenides, whose static conception of Being underlies Plato's discomfort with the Heraclitean flux he examines here. Protagoras and Heraclitus themselves (treated in earlier chapters of the book) supply the two rival doctrines -- relativism and universal flux -- that the dialogue tests and criticizes.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The dispute over whether knowledge can be reduced to sense-experience anticipates the entire empiricist tradition (which the chapter's opening line calls the view 'most modern men take for granted'), while Plato's opposing insistence that genuine knowledge concerns fixed concepts anticipates rationalist epistemology. Russell explicitly connects the fallacy about a predicate of a predicate being a predicate of the subject, and the treatment of 'existence,' to problems taken up centuries later in the philosophy of logic, including the ontological argument for God's existence.
religion_science_culture_context: Russell draws a scientific parallel at one point, noting that modern quantum physics permits change of quality without change of substance -- a possibility neither Plato nor the Ephesian Heracliteans considered, and which Plato would have thought (wrongly, in the event) fatal to science.
russell_presentation: Russell treats the first half of the Theaetetus as Plato's careful, largely negative examination of the claim that knowledge is perception. He reconstructs three linked theses under examination -- knowledge is perception, man is the measure of all things, and everything is in flux -- and works through Plato's arguments and the objections raised against each. He credits Plato with a genuinely serious final argument (that knowledge requires apprehending existence, likeness, and number, none of which is delivered by any single sense), but subjects each strand of Plato's case to close logical scrutiny of his own: he defends judgements of likeness and unlikeness as legitimate perceptual data (accusing Plato of ignoring the cortex), dismantles the treatment of 'existence' as a syntactic confusion, and analyses number-words as 'logical fictions' rather than Platonic entities. He concludes that, aside from the special, purely formal case of logic and mathematics, Plato's arguments against basing all knowledge on perception are fallacious -- though this failure does not prove the perception theory of knowledge true, only that Plato has not disproved it validly. Russell also faults Plato for caricaturing the doctrine of flux in its most extreme form and for assimilating too much of ordinary knowledge to the model of mathematics under Pythagorean influence.
critical_context: Common scholarly caveat: Russell's reconstruction reads the Theaetetus through the lens of his own logical apparatus (theory of descriptions, 'judgements of perception,' numbers as logical constructions), developed decades after Plato wrote. Many Plato scholars treat this as illuminating but anachronistic -- useful for testing the validity of Plato's arguments, but not necessarily capturing what Plato himself meant by 'existence,' 'likeness,' or the soul's apprehension of them, which are embedded in his wider (and here largely suppressed) theory of Forms.
key_takeaways: The Theaetetus tests and ultimately rejects the definition 'knowledge is perception,' without settling on any positive definition of knowledge.
Socrates links this definition to Protagoras's relativism ('man is the measure of all things') and to Heraclitus's doctrine of universal flux.
Pushed to an extreme, universal flux makes any definite assertion -- including assertions about perception itself -- impossible, since words need at least temporarily fixed meanings.

Plato's strongest argument is that knowledge requires grasping existence, likeness/unlikeness, and number, none of which is delivered by any single sense-organ, so knowledge cannot be mere perception.

Russell answers that likeness and unlikeness can be genuine perceptual data, that 'existence' as a predicate of things (rather than descriptions) is a syntactic confusion, and that numbers are 'logical fictions,' formal rather than Platonic entities.
Only pure mathematics, in Russell's assessment, is genuinely independent of perception; Plato's extension of this independence to all knowledge is unproven, not merely wrong.
study_notes:
The key move to track in this chapter is Russell's habit of separating what is logically sound in an ancient argument from what merely sounds plausible. Plato's dialogue raises a genuinely hard question -- can perception alone deliver comparison, existence, and number? -- and Russell takes the question seriously rather than dismissing it. But he then applies tools unavailable to Plato (the analysis of 'exists' as a predicate only of descriptions, and of numbers as patterns rather than objects) to show that Plato's inference from 'the senses don't perceive existence' to 'therefore only the mind, using a wholly separate faculty, can know existence' does not go through: there may simply be no such 'thing' as existence for anything, sense-perceived or otherwise, to 'be' in the sense Plato assumes.

Notice also how the chapter uses the flux argument as a cautionary example about extremism in philosophy: taking a true insight (things do change) and pushing it to its most extreme, univocal form (everything changes in every way, all the time) produces self-refuting nonsense, since even the claim itself could not be stated. Russell's own moderate position -- that word-meanings must be fixed only 'at least for a time' -- is a useful general lesson for evaluating any philosophical doctrine that seems to prove too much.

Finally, watch how Russell handles Plato's treatment of mathematics. He does not deny that arithmetic is independent of the senses; he agrees with Plato on that much. What he denies is that this special, formal independence can be generalized to ordinary empirical knowledge -- a distinction Plato, under the influence of Pythagorean mathematical mysticism, tends to blur.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A raw bit of sensory experience -- like a patch of colour or a sound -- before it has been interpreted or put into words.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Russell's usage, the bare occurrence given in sensation, belonging equally to the physical and the psychological orders, which is in itself neither true nor false and therefore cannot by itself constitute knowledge.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: What you get once you put a raw sensation into words or connect it with memory -- for example, judging 'this shade of red is like that one.'
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's term for a percept 'filled out' with words and memories, and thereby rendered capable of truth or falsehood; he argues the thesis 'knowledge is perception' is defensible only if reinterpreted as 'knowledge is judgements of perception.'

glossary_terms.term: Man is the measure of all things
glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Protagoras's saying that things are, for each person, exactly as they seem to that person -- there's no independent standard beyond individual perception.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Protagorean relativism, identified by Socrates in the Theaetetus with the doctrine that knowledge is perception; tested and largely rejected on the grounds that it cannot account for cases (such as a doctor's or statesman's foresight) where one judgement is genuinely more reliable than another.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The Heraclitean idea that absolutely everything is constantly changing, in every respect, all the time.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine, radicalized by Heraclitus's Ephesian disciples in the Theaetetus, that a thing changes both in place and in every quality without cessation, which Plato shows destroys the fixity of meaning needed for any coherent assertion.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Something that seems, from ordinary language, to be a 'thing' (like the number two) but which, once the sentence using it is properly analysed, turns out not to correspond to any single object at all.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Russell's term for entities such as numbers, which are not constituents of the facts that verify statements about them but only common logical forms; e.g. 'I have two hands' contains, on analysis, no constituent corresponding to the word 'two.'

questions.prompt: What definition of 'knowledge' does Theaetetus propose at the start of the dialogue, and with which sophist's doctrine does Socrates identify it?
questions.answer: Theaetetus proposes that 'knowledge is nothing but perception.' Socrates identifies this with Protagoras's doctrine that 'man is the measure of all things.'
questions.explanation: This identification is the hinge of the whole dialogue: testing 'knowledge is perception' becomes, in large part, testing Protagorean relativism.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, why does the extreme version of the Heraclitean flux doctrine make it impossible even to say 'this is white'?
questions.answer: If everything is changing in every respect at every instant, then whatever was white when the sentence began will have ceased to be white before the sentence is finished, so the statement can never be straightforwardly true.
questions.explanation: This shows that some minimal fixity of meaning, for at least a short time, is required for any assertion -- including assertions about flux itself -- to be possible.

questions.prompt: Compare Plato's argument that existence cannot be known through the senses with Russell's own analysis of the word 'exists.'
questions.answer: Plato argues that we have a single thought including both sound and colour, namely that they 'exist,' and that no sense-organ delivers this; existence must therefore be grasped by the mind alone, without which we could not reach truth. Russell responds that this rests on bad syntax: 'exists' properly applies only to descriptions (e.g. 'the largest lion in the Zoo'), not to a thing pointed out directly; it is nonsense to say of a perceived particular 'this exists,' though it is fine to say 'lions exist' (there are lions). On Russell's view, there is therefore no special mental faculty needed to apprehend 'existence' as a further fact about things.
questions.explanation: This comparison illustrates the chapter's central method: taking an ancient argument seriously, then applying modern logical analysis to test whether its key term is even coherent.

questions.prompt: What objection does Socrates raise, on behalf of common sense, against extending Protagorean relativism to inference and the future?
questions.answer: A doctor genuinely foretells the course of a patient's illness better than the patient does, and in political disputes some people's judgements about the state's future needs prove more accurate than others'; therefore a wise man is, in fact, a better measure of things than a fool, contrary to strict Protagorean equality of judgement.
questions.explanation: This is Plato's key argument for treating inference, unlike bare perception, as answerable to an impersonal standard of correctness.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Plato's final argument against identifying knowledge with perception, based on existence, likeness, and number.
questions.answer: Premise 1: We perceive sound and colour through separate sense-organs, but no sense-organ perceives that they both exist, or that they are alike or unlike, or how many there are. Premise 2: Knowledge of existence, likeness/unlikeness, and number is essential to knowledge. Premise 3: Only the mind, by its own instrumentality, can reach existence and number. Conclusion: Since perception cannot reach existence, and truth cannot be reached without reaching existence, perception cannot be knowledge; knowledge must consist in reflection rather than sense-impression.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as Plato's most serious argument in the dialogue, though he goes on to challenge each of its premises in turn.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Russell, is arithmetic ('2 + 2 = 4') independent of perception in a way that a statement like 'I have ten fingers' is not?
questions.answer: Pure mathematics consists of tautologies about the meanings of symbols (such as 'or,' 'not,' 'all,' 'some'), which can be known to be correct without studying the world at all. 'I have ten fingers,' by contrast, is a proposition of enumeration: the concept 'finger' is abstracted from perception, and although the number-word 'ten' can be analysed away formally, the underlying fact it describes is still, in part, a matter of perceiving actual fingers.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this distinction to concede what is right in Plato's claim that mathematics is not derived from the senses, while denying that this supports Plato's broader claim about all knowledge.

flashcards.front: What definition of knowledge does Theaetetus first propose?
With whose doctrine does Socrates identify 'knowledge is perception'?
flashcards.back: Protagoras's doctrine that 'man is the measure of all things.'

flashcards.front: What does Socrates add to Protagoras's doctrine, from Heraclitus?
flashcards.back: The doctrine that everything is always changing -- that 'all the things we are pleased to say "are" really are in process of becoming.'

flashcards.front: What example does Socrates give of perception changing with the percipient rather than the object?
flashcards.back: He finds wine sweet when well, but sour when ill.

flashcards.front: What is the 'pigs and baboons' objection to Protagoras?
flashcards.back: If man is the measure of all things because he perceives, pigs and baboons -- also percipients -- should equally be measures of all things.

flashcards.front: What proto-pragmatist defense does Socrates offer on Protagoras's behalf?
flashcards.back: That one judgement cannot be truer than another, but can be 'better,' in having better consequences.

flashcards.front: What refutes the idea that no one's judgement can be wiser than another's, according to Socrates?
flashcards.back: A doctor genuinely knows more about the future course of a patient's illness than the patient does.

flashcards.front: What happens to the meanings of words under the extreme Heraclitean flux doctrine, according to Plato's argument?
flashcards.back: Nothing can be truly called 'white' or 'seeing' rather than 'not-white' or 'not-seeing,' since everything changes in every way at every instant -- so no assertion can be definitely true.

flashcards.front: How does Plato/Socrates react when asked to discuss Parmenides directly?
flashcards.back: He refuses, calling Parmenides 'a reverend and awful figure' and 'one being whom I respect above all,' and does not develop the Parmenidean alternative.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's distinction between a 'percept' and a 'judgement of perception'?
flashcards.back: A percept is a bare occurrence, neither true nor false; a judgement of perception is a percept filled out with words and memory, and so capable of truth or falsehood.

flashcards.front: How does Russell analyse the sentence 'lions exist'?
flashcards.back: As 'there are lions,' i.e. "'x is a lion' is true for a suitable x" -- 'exists' applies to a description, not to a thing pointed out directly.

flashcards.front: What does Russell mean by calling numbers 'logical fictions'?
flashcards.back: Number-words like 'two' correspond to no single constituent in the facts they describe; what different 'there are two so-and-sos' statements share is only a common logical form, not a common object.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's final verdict on Plato's arguments in this dialogue?
flashcards.back: Only mathematics and logic are genuinely independent of perception; Plato's arguments extending this to all knowledge are fallacious -- which shows his conclusion unproven, not necessarily false.

False
quiz.explanation: If everything changes in every way at every instant, no assertion (including 'this is white') can remain true long enough to be stated -- word-meanings must be fixed at least for a time.
quiz.related_concept: Universal flux (Heraclitean doctrine applied to sense-objects)

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's central objection to Plato's claim that no sense-organ perceives likeness and unlikeness?
options: That likeness is a Platonic Idea, not a percept
That Plato ignores the cortex and wrongly assumes all sense-organs are at the body's surface
That Heraclitus already refuted this claim
That likeness cannot be true or false
quiz.explanation: Russell argues likeness/unlikeness between simultaneously perceived colours can be part of the perceptual datum itself, a 'judgement of perception.'

quiz.prompt: How does Russell analyse the statement 'lions exist,' as against Plato's treatment of existence as directly perceived by the mind?
options: As a synthetic a priori judgement
As meaning 'there are lions,' i.e. that 'x is a lion' is true for a suitable x -- 'exists' applies to descriptions, not to things pointed out directly
As an innate idea implanted by God
As identical in meaning to 'lions are perceived'
quiz.explanation: Russell treats Plato's claim about a special faculty perceiving 'existence' as resting on a syntactic confusion about how the word 'exists' functions.
quiz.related_concept: 'Existence' as bad syntax (the critique of predicating existence of things)

quiz.prompt: What does Russell mean by calling numbers 'logical fictions'?
options: That numbers do not exist even as symbols
That number-words correspond to no single shared constituent across the facts they describe, but only to a common logical form
That Plato invented the concept of number
That arithmetic is derived entirely from sense-perception
quiz.explanation: Russell shows that 'I have two hands' can be restated without the word 'two' occurring at all, using only quantifiers and identity -- so 'two' names no single thing.

quiz.prompt: Socrates refuses to discuss Parmenides directly, calling him 'a reverend and awful figure' and 'one being whom I respect above ____.'
options: all
Heraclitus
Protagoras
the gods
quiz.explanation: The phrase reveals Plato's underlying preference for a static Parmenidean universe over the flux he is provisionally defending for the sake of argument.
quiz.related_concept: Universal flux (Heraclitean doctrine applied to sense-objects)

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Plato's final argument that knowledge cannot be perception because perception cannot apprehend existence, likeness, or number. Using Russell's own responses, assess whether each of Plato's premises survives scrutiny.
rubric: Accurately states Plato's argument and its premises
Explains Russell's counter-argument regarding likeness/unlikeness as perceptual data
Explains Russell's syntactic critique of 'existence' as a predicate
Reaches a reasoned overall verdict on whether the argument succeeds

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Protagorean relativism and the extreme Heraclitean flux doctrine as they function in the Theaetetus: what problem does each pose for the definition 'knowledge is perception,' and how are they related to each other in Plato's argument?
rubric: Correctly explains Protagorean relativism and its main objections
Correctly explains the flux doctrine and how it undermines fixed assertion
Clarifies how Socrates links the two doctrines together in the dialogue
Uses specific textual details (e.g. the doctor argument, the wine example)
